newsitem.title: JAPAN: DVDs, lacking software, may attract few customers.
newsitem.headline: DVDs, lacking software, may attract few customers.

text.p: A new super compact disc system, the digital video disc (DVD), will hit the Japanese market on Thursday, but consumers may be frustrated to find few software titles for the DVD players on store shelves.

Despite a sales blitz by Matsushita Electric Industrial Co and Toshiba Corp, only about 15 software titles will be available on November 1, when the two makers will launch DVD players for the first time in the world, industry sources said.
None of the Hollywood hits will be among them.
Industry analysts agree on the big market potential of the DVDs and expect the product to eventually make compact discs and videocassette recorders obsolete.
However, they say the sales of DVD players will remain slow in the Christmas season and next year.
"It will only be people like gadget freaks who will buy DVDs this year, due in part to the lack of software," said Yoshiharu Izumi, analyst at UBS Securities Ltd.

DVDs, developed by the world's top 10 electronics firms and film makers including Matsushita and Toshiba, can store up to seven times more data in a single disc than a conventional compact disc and can easily store a full-length movie.
The DVD system is also expected to spawn a host of multimedia software titles, replacing the CD-ROMs used in most personal computers.
Matsushita and Toshiba, which have continuously run full-page advertisements in major newspapers, set recommended prices for the players at 79,800 yen ($706) and 77,000 yen ($681), respectively.
Other DVD developers, including Pioneer Electronic Corp, Hitachi Ltd, and Sony Corp, will launch their players later this year or early next year.
However, some recording companies' announcements that they would delay the release of their software titles threw cold water on the makers' sales efforts, analysts said.
Toshiba EMI, Victor Entertainment Co and Pony Canyon Inc said they would delay the release of five software titles for one or two weeks due to technical problems.
"We want to make doubly sure that all DVD players are compatible with each other," Toshiba EMI said in a statement.
Last-minute changes in copyright protection measures in negotiations between hardware and software makers caused the delay in technology development at software makers, some analysts said.
